extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, examiners, and researchers analyzing patentability and patent-quality metrics
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and quality dimensions for determining whether an invention/patent application is patentable (and distinctions for utility models), together with related evaluation metrics used in patent-quality reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To be patentable a technical solution must be (1) new, (2) involve an inventive step, and (3) be industrially applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion is the core legal threshold used to evaluate inventions. Evaluators/examiners assess novelty (absence of prior art), inventive step (non‑obviousness over prior art), and industrial applicability (usefulness/practical application).

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility model eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility models protect inventions which are new and industrially applicable; they do not need an inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used where jurisdictions offer utility model protection: the standard is lower than for patents because inventive_step/non-obviousness is not required, making utility models suitable for incremental innovations. Term and renewal rules differ by jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must be new (not anticipated by prior art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess prior disclosures, publications, and existing products. Any single prior art reference that discloses all essential features can defeat novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step (non-obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must involve an inventive step — it should not be obvious to a person skilled in the art in view of prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment typically considers combinations of prior art and whether the claimed advance would have been an obvious modification. Examiner reasoning and problem-solution approaches can be applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial applicability (usefulness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must be capable of industrial application (i.e., it can be made or used in some kind of industry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often requires that the specification enable at least one practical application; abstract or purely theoretical ideas that cannot be implemented will fail this criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of disclosure (support/enablement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications should provide sufficient description, examples, and details so the invention can be carried out by a person skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While explicit '§112' style language is not visible in this chunk, the document emphasizes descriptive completeness (claims supported by specification); lack of enablement or missing essential information can be grounds for rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiated evaluation by protection type
rubrics_metrics.description: Different protection forms (patents vs. utility models) are evaluated against different legal thresholds and quality metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When measuring or reporting patent quality, treat patents and utility models separately (e.g., patentability strictness, procedural timelines, and rights duration differ).
